category.text: $course$/Containerization in AWS/Track A — ECS & Fargate Quiz

questiontext.text: The course VPC has no NAT Gateway. Your containers run in the public subnets with public IPs, and only RDS sits in the private subnets. What is the main reason the containers can't simply run in the private subnets?

answer.text: Without a NAT Gateway, nothing in a private subnet can reach ECR or AWS APIs, so the containers couldn't pull their images
An Application Load Balancer can only send traffic to targets in public subnets
RDS only accepts connections from resources in public subnets
Private subnets are billed per hour, while public subnets are free

questiontext.text: dcta-rds-sg allows port 5432 from dcta-app-sg rather than from the app subnets' IP ranges. Given that you destroy and re-create your containers every session, what is the key benefit?

answer.text: The rule keeps working even though the containers get new IP addresses every session, and it only covers resources that wear the app security group
Security-group references are checked faster than IP ranges, so database queries are quicker
RDS does not support IP-range rules on port 5432
It lets the database be reached from the internet, but only by the app

questiontext.text: In infra/20-data you read the DB password with an ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" block. Which way of passing it to aws_db_instance works?

answer.text: password_wo (with password_wo_version) — ephemeral values may only go into write-only arguments, which are never saved to state
password — Terraform encrypts it automatically because it came from an ephemeral block
password with sensitive = true on the argument, which keeps it out of state
username — RDS reads the password from Secrets Manager once it knows the user

questiontext.text: On a fresh RDS for PostgreSQL 17 instance, the backend logs no pg_hba.conf entry … no encryption. The security groups are correct. What is the cause?

answer.text: RDS for PostgreSQL 15 and later require TLS by default (rds.force_ssl = 1), and the app is connecting without it
Port 5432 is blocked, so the connection falls back to an unencrypted port
The password in Secrets Manager doesn't match the database
The DB subnet group uses public subnets, which RDS refuses

questiontext.text: You built and pushed the backend image from an Apple Silicon Mac with a plain docker build. The image is in ECR, the task pulls it, and then stops immediately with exec format error. What went wrong?

answer.text: The image was built for arm64, but AWS runs it on amd64 — rebuild with --platform linux/amd64 and push a new tag
The start script in the image isn't executable — add chmod +x in the Dockerfile
The task execution role can't pull from ECR
The tag is immutable, so ECS refused to overwrite the running container

questiontext.text: Your backend service uses FARGATE_SPOT weight 7 and FARGATE weight 3, with desired_count = 1. describe-tasks shows a single FARGATE_SPOT task. What does this tell you?

answer.text: Nothing is wrong — one task is either Spot or not, so the 70/30 mix only becomes visible when the service runs more tasks
The strategy is broken — ECS should have split the task 70/30 between both providers
The weights must add up to 100 (70 and 30), so ECS ignored them
FARGATE_SPOT always wins until the account runs out of Spot capacity

questiontext.text: The backend's task definition gets DB_PASSWORD through its secrets block. The app code itself never calls AWS. Which IAM role actually reads the secret?

answer.text: The task execution role, used by ECS before your code starts
The backend's task role, because the variable ends up inside the backend container
The ECS infrastructure role for load balancers
The GitLab CI role, when it registers the task definition

questiontext.text: Your listener has one rule, path pattern /api/* → backend, and a default action → frontend. Where does a request for exactly /api (no trailing slash) go?

answer.text: To the frontend, through the default action — /api/* doesn't match /api on its own
To the backend — the ALB adds the trailing slash before matching
Nowhere — the ALB returns 404 because no rule matched
To both target groups, split evenly

questiontext.text: You scale dcta-backend to 0 tasks. The /api/* rule still exists. What does GET /api/tasks return?

answer.text: 503 — the rule matched, but its target group has no targets
200 with the React page — the ALB falls back to the default action when a target group is empty
404 from the ALB, because the backend path no longer exists
A timeout, because the security group still allows the old task IP

questiontext.text: GitLab CI has just deployed task definition revision 7 to dcta-backend. The service has no lifecycle { ignore_changes = [task_definition] }. You now run terraform apply on 30-track-a for an unrelated change. What happens?

answer.text: Terraform points the service back at the revision it knows about, undoing the pipeline's deployment
Nothing — Terraform never looks at which revision a service is using
Terraform fails with a drift error and refuses to apply
Terraform adopts revision 7 as its own and keeps it

name.text: CA11 — Keyless CI on a Feature Branch

questiontext.text: Your CI logs in to AWS with GitLab OIDC. The dcta-gitlab-ci role trusts gitlab.com:sub = project_path:<group>/<project>:ref_type:branch:ref:main. A job on the branch feature/login fails with not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Why?

answer.text: The job's token says it's from feature/login, and the role only trusts tokens from the main branch
The AWS access key stored in GitLab has expired
OIDC tokens only work in scheduled pipelines
The role's permissions don't include ecr:GetAuthorizationToken

questiontext.text: The backend auto-scales on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization with a target of 70%. It's running 3 tasks at 90%, 20% and 20% CPU. What will auto scaling do?

answer.text: Not scale out — the service average is about 43%, below the 70% target
Scale out, because one task is above 70%
Replace the 90% task with a new one
Scale out to the maximum at once, because one task is 20 points over the target

questiontext.text: The frontend uses rolling updates with minimum healthy 100%, maximum 200%, and the deployment circuit breaker with rollback. You push an image that crashes on start. What do users see?

answer.text: No errors — the old task keeps serving while the new ones fail, and ECS rolls back by itself
A short burst of 503s while ECS swaps the old task for the new one
Errors until someone rolls back by hand — the circuit breaker only sends an alert
The ALB sends traffic to the crashing task until its health check fails three times

name.text: CA14 — Two Answers During a Deploy

questiontext.text: During a blue/green deployment of the backend, curl /api/tasks returns the old version, but curl -H 'X-Deploy-Stage: test' /api/tasks returns the new one. Why?

answer.text: A higher-priority test rule matches the header and forwards to the alternate target group where the new tasks run; the production rule hasn't switched yet
The ALB caches the old response for requests without custom headers
Sticky sessions keep normal users on the old tasks until they log out
The header sends the request to a second load balancer that ECS created for the deployment

questiontext.text: Both the production and test listener rules carry lifecycle { ignore_changes = [action] }. Why?

answer.text: ECS rewrites where the rules forward during blue/green deployments; without it, the next terraform apply would point traffic back at the old target group
The ALB API doesn't allow Terraform to update a rule's action after it's created
It lets you change rule priorities without recreating the rules
It stops Terraform from deleting the rules during terraform destroy
